title: Watching an error budget burn
sub: 28 days of a 99.9% SLO: background errors, one incident, one slow leak.

frames.caption: SLO: 99.9% of requests succeed over 28 days. With a million requests a day, the error budget is 28,000 failed requests. The dashed line is a burn rate of 1: spending the budget exactly evenly. Normal background errors (0.04%) burn at 0.4×, comfortably below it.

Day 9: a bad deploy fails 1.5% of requests for two hours. Burn rate = error rate ÷ (1 − SLO) = 15×. At that pace the whole month's budget would be gone in under two days. A fast-burn alert (burn rate above 14.4× over the last hour, as in Google's SRE workbook) pages someone immediately (red). The incident still costs 4% of the month's budget.

Days 18 to 21: a slow leak at 0.25% errors, a burn rate of 2.5×. No single hour looks dramatic, so a fast-burn alert would never fire. A slow-burn alert (above 1× sustained over hours) opens a ticket instead (orange). Over three days this leak costs 27% of the budget: more than the incident.

The window ends with 33% of the budget left, so the SLO was met. Had it run out, the team would freeze risky launches and spend the time on reliability. Burn-rate alerts are what make the budget usable in practice: they fire on how fast the budget is going, not on every individual error.
